name: The Leidenfrost Effect
statement: On a surface far hotter than boiling, a water droplet rides its own vapor and lingers.
statementAccent: a water droplet rides its own vapor and lingers
meaning: The Leidenfrost effect is a phenomenon in which a liquid brought near a surface much hotter than its boiling point produces an insulating layer of vapor that keeps the liquid from boiling away rapidly and lets it hover above the surface. The most familiar example is water droplets sprinkled on a very hot skillet: instead of hissing and vanishing almost instantly, they bead up, skitter and dance across the surface, and last far longer than droplets on a cooler pan. This counterintuitive result, that hotter can mean slower to evaporate, occurs because the droplet floats on a cushion of its own vapor that insulates it from the heat. The effect, also known as film boiling, is named after the German doctor Johann Gottlob Leidenfrost, who described it in 1756. It sets in above a characteristic temperature, the Leidenfrost point, well above the boiling point, and it is important in cooling and quenching, where the insulating vapor film can dramatically reduce heat transfer.
mechanism: When a droplet lands on a surface just above the boiling point, its underside boils vigorously and it evaporates quickly. But when the surface is hotter than the Leidenfrost point, the underside of the droplet flashes to vapor so fast that a continuous thin layer of gas forms between the droplet and the surface. Because this vapor layer has very low thermal conductivity compared with the solid, it insulates the rest of the droplet, sharply reducing the rate at which heat reaches the liquid. The droplet therefore evaporates slowly and, supported by the pressure of the vapor continually generated beneath it, levitates just above the surface, free to glide almost frictionlessly. The temperature at which this stable vapor film first forms is the Leidenfrost point, for water roughly two hundred degrees Celsius, well above its hundred-degree boiling point. Below that point the droplet makes contact and boils away quickly; above it the insulating film keeps the droplet intact far longer. The effect is the film-boiling regime, the point of minimum heat transfer in the progression of boiling.

examples.text: Water flicked onto a very hot pan beads into balls that skitter and last far longer than on a merely warm pan, riding a vapor cushion.
For water the effect sets in around two hundred degrees Celsius, well above boiling; below it the droplet boils away fast.
Liquid nitrogen spilled on skin rolls off harmlessly, and, dangerously, a wetted hand briefly dipped in molten metal can be protected by the vapor film.

variants.name: Film boiling
variants.text: The regime in which a stable insulating vapor film separates the liquid from a very hot surface, the physical basis of the effect.

variants.name: The Leidenfrost point
variants.text: The threshold temperature above the boiling point at which the vapor film becomes stable and the effect begins.

whyItMatters: The Leidenfrost effect is a striking and instructive phenomenon that connects a kitchen curiosity to important physics and engineering. Its counterintuitive lesson, that a hotter surface can make a droplet evaporate more slowly, illustrates how an insulating vapor layer governs heat transfer, and it is a vivid demonstration of the different regimes of boiling. In engineering the effect is critical to cooling and quenching processes: when a hot metal is quenched in liquid, a Leidenfrost vapor film can form and drastically slow cooling, and the related boiling crisis, where a surface suddenly enters film boiling, is a key safety concern in the cooling of nuclear reactors and other high-heat systems, since the insulating film can cause overheating. The effect also enables curiosities and demonstrations, from droplets self-propelling on textured hot surfaces to the safe handling of cryogenic liquids. As a clear window into film boiling and heat-transfer limits, the Leidenfrost effect is both a memorable teaching example and a matter of practical consequence.

working.lead: Heat the surface past the threshold
working.text: raise the surface above the Leidenfrost point, well beyond the liquid's boiling temperature.
let the droplet's underside vaporize instantly into a continuous low-conductivity gas layer beneath it.
watch the droplet float on its vapor, insulated so it evaporates slowly and lasts far longer than expected.

limits: The Leidenfrost effect requires the surface to be above the Leidenfrost point, a threshold that depends on the liquid, the surface material and texture, and conditions, so the exact temperature is not universal; for water it is roughly two hundred degrees Celsius but varies. Below that point the effect does not occur and the liquid boils away quickly. The insulating vapor film that makes droplets last longer is the same film that dangerously reduces cooling in quenching and can cause the boiling crisis, so the effect is beneficial or hazardous depending on context. Some popular demonstrations, such as briefly dipping a wet hand in molten metal, are genuinely dangerous and rely on precise conditions. So the Leidenfrost effect is a well-understood consequence of film boiling, occurring only above a surface-dependent threshold and carrying real risks as well as curiosities.
misreadings: The Leidenfrost effect does not mean the droplet boils away faster on a hotter surface; the opposite is true, because the insulating vapor film makes it last longer. It requires the surface to exceed the Leidenfrost point, not merely the boiling point, so a pan just above boiling gives fast evaporation, not levitation. And the protective vapor film is not a reason to touch dangerously hot or molten materials, since the conditions are precise and the risks severe, so treating hotter as always faster to evaporate, or the effect as a safe way to touch molten metal, misreads a phenomenon of film boiling above a specific threshold.
origin: Named after the German doctor Johann Gottlob Leidenfrost, who described it in 1756; the insulating vapor film, or film boiling, that levitates a liquid on a surface above the Leidenfrost point.
